executive_summary: The Docker environment hosting the ICS lab has critical security gaps. Five containers (router, caldera, HMI, simulation, plc) run with elevated privileges (CAP_NET_ADMIN, root user) and expose sensitive networks (admin/ICS/DMZ). Image vulnerabilities are rampant: 195 in router, 1404 in caldera, 168 in HMI, 1600 in simulation, and 1599 in plc. The simulation and EWS containers have Docker socket mounts, enabling host-level control. Resource limits are missing across all containers, risking availability. Immediate remediation is required to prevent lateral movement and process disruption.

findings.title: Elevated Capabilities
findings.explanation: CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_NET_RAW allow full network control and raw socket access, which could enable an attacker to manipulate routing tables or perform network-based attacks on the ICS network.
findings.remediation: Remove unnecessary capabilities by setting CapDrop instead of CapAdd in Docker Compose or CLI.

findings.title: Image Vulnerabilities
findings.explanation: The container image contains 195 high/critical vulnerabilities in core packages like perl, OpenSSL, and network utilities. Exploitation could lead to privilege escalation or network disruption in the ICS environment.
findings.remediation: Rebuild the image with updated packages or switch to a hardened base image. Apply network restrictions to limit exposure.

findings.title: Root Privileges
findings.explanation: Running as root increases risk of privilege escalation if any vulnerabilities exist in the container's software stack.
findings.remediation: Set a non-root user in Docker Compose or Dockerfile using the 'user' directive.

findings.title: Missing Resource Limits
findings.explanation: Unbounded CPU and memory usage could allow resource exhaustion attacks against the ICS network.
findings.remediation: Add CPU and memory limits in Docker Compose or CLI with --memory and --cpu-shares.

findings.title: Docker Socket Mounts
findings.explanation: Mounting the Docker socket in simulation and EWS containers grants full host control. A compromised container could manipulate other containers or the host OS.
findings.remediation: Remove Docker socket mounts from all containers. Use Docker API access controls or dedicated monitoring tools instead of direct socket access.

rejected.title: Image Vulnerabilities
rejected.explanation: The container image contains 7 critical and 157 high-severity vulnerabilities in core packages like OpenSSL, libxml2, and Python. Simulation containers often run long-term processes; a compromised simulation could disrupt ICS operations or act as a pivot point.
rejected.remediation: Rebuild the image with updated packages (e.g., OpenSSL 3.0.19+, libxml2 2.10.4+). Remove the Docker socket mount and isolate the container to the ICS network only.

rejected.title: Multi-Network Bridging
rejected.explanation: Containers bridge admin, ICS, and DMZ networks, violating OT segmentation principles. A compromised container could pivot between network segments, targeting critical ICS components.
rejected.remediation: Implement strict network isolation: admin network only for management services, ICS network only for process systems, and DMZ for external access. Use Docker network policies to enforce segmentation.

recommendations: Isolate ICS containers to dedicated networks with no cross-segment communication (admin/ICS/DMZ separation).
Remove CAP_NET_ADMIN and other unnecessary capabilities from all containers.
Set non-root users in Docker Compose files (user directive) for all containers.
Add CPU and memory limits to all containers to prevent resource exhaustion.
Rebuild all images with updated packages (e.g., OpenSSL 3.0.19+, Python 3.11.10+).
Remove Docker socket mounts from simulation and EWS containers.
